title: Post-Course Portfolio: Online Connect Four / Battleship
descriptionMarkdown:
# Online Connect Four / Battleship

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after the Real-Time Online Tic-Tac-Toe project, whose WebSocket connection handling and turn-validation pattern this project extends into a larger board and, for Battleship specifically, a phase where each player has genuinely hidden information the other must never see.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`connect-four-checkpoint`** ("Gravity-drop connect four engine"), a pure in-memory `ConnectFourEngine.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the gravity-drop, turn-validation, and four-in-a-row-detection core. Passing its hidden tests proves your game logic is correct, independent of any real WebSocket transport. If you choose Battleship instead of Connect Four, port the same turn-validation and win-detection discipline to your own ship-placement and shot logic; the checkpoint's Connect Four contract is what is graded either way, as the required proof of a correctly generalized turn-based engine.

The real-time delivery over a WebSocket connection, and — for Battleship — the actual hidden-ship-placement confidentiality enforcement, are external and self-reviewed.

## Beyond what the lessons taught

This project assumes the WebSocket research already done for Tic-Tac-Toe. Pick one game (Connect Four is the simpler choice; Battleship is harder because of the hidden-ship-placement phase) rather than building both.

## Architecture overview

```text
GameWebSocketHandler            <- accepts connections, matches players, routes drop/shot messages
GameSession                      <- your checkpoint's board/turn/win rules, reshaped as a stateful session object
PlayerView projection             <- for Battleship: the per-player broadcast view, stripped of the opponent's unrevealed ships
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a session object.** Carry your gravity-drop/turn/win rules (or your Battleship equivalent) into `GameSession`, unit tests unchanged.
2. **Slice 2 — a two-player session and the authoritative board.** Hold the full authoritative state server-side; for Connect Four, broadcast the same board to both players after each drop.
3. **Slice 3 — win detection, checked incrementally.** Check for four-in-a-row (or all-ships-sunk) only around the most recent move, not by rescanning the entire board every time.
4. **Slice 4 — for Battleship: the private placement phase and view stripping.** Validate placement server-side (no overlap, no off-board), then build each player's broadcast view by stripping the opponent's unrevealed ship cells before sending.
5. **Slice 5 — disconnect handling.** Reuse the same documented policy and test approach as the Tic-Tac-Toe project.

## Common pitfalls

- **Rescanning the whole board for a win after every move.** Check only the lines passing through the most recently placed piece; Chapter 10's complexity discipline applies directly here.
- **For Battleship: relying on the client UI to hide the opponent's ships instead of stripping them server-side.** Build and inspect the actual outgoing message, not just what the UI happens to render.
- **Validating ship placement only on the client.** Re-validate overlap and board-bounds server-side; a client can send anything.
- **Reusing the Tic-Tac-Toe session object unchanged instead of adapting its win-check and turn logic to the new board size and rules.** The shape of the state machine transfers; the specific board and win logic does not.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Play a full game to completion over two real WebSocket connections and confirm both clients see a consistent final board.
- For Battleship: capture the raw WebSocket messages sent to one player during a full game and confirm the opponent's unrevealed ship cells never appear in any of them.
- Attempt an out-of-turn or invalid move/shot and confirm the board broadcast to both players is unaffected.

## Required evidence

- A win/game-over detection test suite (four-in-a-row in all four directions for Connect Four, or all-ships-sunk for Battleship).
- For Battleship specifically: a test proving a player's outgoing broadcast never contains the opponent's unrevealed ship-position data, inspected at the JSON/message level, not just "the UI doesn't display it."
- A ship-placement validation test suite (overlapping ships rejected, off-board placement rejected) if you chose Battleship, or a column-full rejection test if you chose Connect Four.
- A concurrency test for two near-simultaneous moves/shots in the same session, confirming turn order is enforced correctly.
- The same disconnect-handling documentation and test as the Tic-Tac-Toe project, adapted to this game.

## Review and completion

A reviewer plays a full game to completion, then — for Battleship specifically — inspects the raw WebSocket messages sent to one player during the game and confirms the other player's ship positions never appeared in any message before being legitimately revealed by a hit.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded gravity-drop connect four engine checkpoint and extend a validated turn-based architecture to a larger board and richer win conditions
Enforce per-player information asymmetry at the server boundary, never relying on the client to hide data
Validate a private setup phase (ship placement) server-side before gameplay begins
Efficiently check a win condition incrementally rather than rescanning the entire board on every move
Inspect raw outgoing messages, not just the UI, to verify a confidentiality requirement actually holds
